content: The following institutions and entities are responsible for monitoring and implementing policies related to the health workforce: 1. National and Regional Ministries of Health: These governmental bodies oversee the health sector at both national and regional levels, ensuring the implementation of health policies and workforce management. 2. Professional Chambers: These organizations represent health professionals, regulate their practice, and contribute to workforce planning and policy development. 3. Institutions or Units Responsible for Monitoring Health Workforce Policies: These entities are tasked with collecting and analyzing data related to the health workforce, including its size, distribution, and capacity. 4. Ministry of Labour: This ministry plays a role in workforce planning, particularly in relation to labor market dynamics and employment policies. 5. National Statistical Offices: These offices collect and report data on the health workforce, contributing to evidence-based policy-making. Indicator: Ability of HRHIS to Track Entrants to the Labor Market This indicator assesses whether the Health Resource Information System (HRHIS) can generate data to monitor new entrants into the health labor market. The indicator is categorized as Yes, No, or Partly, depending on the system's functionality. It is related to the collection of flow data for labor market entry indicators, as outlined in Module 05 – Health Labor Market Flows. By 2020, all countries were expected to have made progress in establishing registries to track health workforce stock, education, distribution, flows, demand, capacity, and remuneration. To evaluate this indicator, the following questions should be addressed: 1. Is there a system that provides information about the health workforce? 2. If yes, does this system provide information on the inflows of the health labor market? Indicator: Ability of HRHIS to Track Active Stock in the Labor Market This indicator evaluates whether the HRHIS can generate data to monitor the active stock of health workers in the labor market. It is categorized as Yes, No, or Partly, based on the system's capabilities. The indicator is linked to the collection of stock data for labor market entry indicators, as described in Module 01 – Active Health Workforce Stock. By 2020, all countries were expected to have established systems to track health workforce stock, education, distribution, flows, demand, capacity, and remuneration. To assess this indicator, the following questions should be considered: 1. Is there a health workforce information system that provides data on the health workforce? 2. If yes, does this system provide information on the stock of the health labor market? Indicator: Ability of HRHIS to Track Exits from the Labor Market This indicator measures whether the HRHIS can generate data to monitor exits from the health labor market. It is categorized as Yes, No, or Partly, depending on the system's functionality. The indicator is associated with the collection of flow data for labor market exit indicators, as outlined in Module 05 – Health Labor Market Flows. By 2020, all countries were expected to have made progress in establishing registries to track health workforce stock, education, distribution, flows, demand, capacity, and remuneration. To evaluate this indicator, the following questions should be addressed: 1. Is there a health workforce information system that provides data on the health workforce? 2. If yes, does this system provide information on the outflows of the health labor market? Indicator: Ability of HRHIS to Generate Geocoded Information on Health Facility Locations This indicator assesses whether the HRHIS can produce geocoded data on the locations of health facilities. It is categorized as Yes, No, or Partly, based on the system's capabilities. The indicator is related to the collection of distribution data for labor market stock indicators, as described in Module 01 – Active Health Workforce Stock. By 2020, all countries were expected to have established systems to track health workforce stock, education, distribution, flows, demand, capacity, and remuneration. To assess this indicator, the following question should be considered: 1. Is there a health workforce information system that provides geocoded data on the locations of health facilities? Data Reporting Frequency and Potential Data Sources Data reporting for these indicators is typically conducted on an annual basis. Potential data sources include: Ministries of Health and subnational health ministries. Institutions or units responsible for monitoring health workforce policies. Organizations collecting data on the health workforce. Development of National Health Workforce Accounts (NHWA) The NHWA indicators were developed through a stepwise process involving consultations with experts and stakeholders. In 2015, over 450 indicators were initially selected from various international and subregional sources. These were filtered down to 255 indicators to eliminate duplicates and ensure comprehensive coverage of underlying concepts. A global consultation (Delphi study) was conducted in November 2015, involving over 70 experts, including academics, policymakers, and health professionals. The indicators were evaluated based on relevance, availability, and utilization in national contexts. The final list of indicators was defined through discussions and workshops at WHO headquarters, ensuring alignment with existing tools and minimizing redundancy in data collection efforts. Key Tools and Data Collection Efforts The NHWA system is built on the WHO Minimum Data Set (MDS) for health workforce registry, published in 2015. This serves as the foundation for Module 1 indicators. The Joint Questionnaire on Non-Monetary Health Care Statistics, harmonized by OECD, Eurostat, and WHO, is an established annual global data collection effort on HRH. This comprehensive approach enables integrated data collection, analysis, and synthesis to inform policy options and improve health workforce planning and management.
